ta-l1d19q2-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph introducing the bases of the persons' equality: eternity and magnitude, with power deferred to Distinction 43. On eternity, beyond Distinction 8, two articles are posed: what eternity is in reality, and how the 'now' of eternity relates to eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3510.summary: First argument that eternity is not the divine substance. Nothing is its own cause, and God is the author of eternity (Augustine) and before eternity as its cause (Liber de causis).
claims: God is called the author of eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3513.summary: Second argument. Each thing is measured by the first in its genus, and the first being is divine being, so all being is measured by its measure. Temporal being is measured by time and eternal beings by aevum, and one thing has only one measure, so eternity is really the same as aevum and time.
claims: All being is measured by the first being's measure.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3516.summary: Third argument. In every participation of divine goodness there is a community of name and concept by analogy between the participated perfection and its source, as creaturely goodness relates to uncreated goodness. According to Dionysius, as God is called wise by filling others with wisdom, he is called eternal as cause of aevum and time, so aevum and time should be called eternity.
claims: Participated perfections share the name of their source analogically.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3520.summary: Fourth argument. A measure is proportioned to what it measures. All being in itself is indivisible, having nothing mixed in (Boethius), and as long as a thing remains its substantial being does not vary, though its accidents do. Since the being of temporal things is measured by time, time would be an indivisible and permanent measure and not differ from eternity.
claims: Substantial being is indivisible and invariant.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3523.summary: Fifth argument. Whatever has succession is measured by time, and the being of aeviternal things, such as angels and the heavenly substance, is not measured by time, so it has no succession and does not differ from eternity.
claims: What has succession is measured by time.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3526.summary: Thomas's determination. Some distinguished time, aevum, and eternity thus: time has beginning and end, aevum beginning but no end, eternity neither. This does not capture their essential difference, since if time had no beginning or end it would still not be eternity (Boethius), and if angels had always existed aevum would still differ from eternity. All three signify duration, and duration follows actuality, since a thing endures as long as it is in act. Being in act is twofold. The act may be incomplete and mixed with potency, proceeding further into act, which is motion, the act of what exists in potency as such. Or the act may be unmixed with potency and admit no addition of perfection, which is quiet, permanent act. This is twofold: the actual being a thing has may be acquired from another, so that the thing is potential relative to an act it has received perfectly; or actual being may belong to a thing of itself, as part of its quiddity, which is divine being, with no potentiality relative to that act. So there are three kinds of act. Act with no underlying potency, divine being and its operation, has eternity as its measure. Complete act acquired in an underlying potency has aevum. Act with an underlying potency mixed with it, proceeding to complete act by succession and receiving added perfection, has time. Since each thing has its proper measure, the essential difference of measures follows the condition of the measured act. In motion there is succession of before and after, and these, as numbered by the soul, are a measure by way of number, time, which is the number of motion according to before and after (the Philosopher). It is a numbered number, as two dogs is a numbered number and two simply a number. What is quasi-material in time, before and after, is founded in motion, and what is formal is completed by the numbering soul, which is why the Philosopher says that without the soul there would be no time. Time requires a plurality, at least two nows with time between or two times joined by a now, and that they succeed one another. Continuity comes to time from the motion it measures, so a non-continuous motion not ordered to the heavens' continuous motion would have a non-continuous time. So time measures only what is included in time by beginning and end: even if the heavens' motion were eternal, each revolution or part, measured by before and after, has beginning and end, and in this sense time has beginning and end. In complete act there is no before and after, no plurality, and no succession, so its measure is by way of unity rather than number. As the numbered before and after complete the concept of time, the permanence of act, understood as one with the character of measure, completes the concept of aevum and eternity. Since aeviternal being is acquired from another, aevum measures being that has a beginning, while eternity measures being not acquired from another. In this way the proposed difference can be sustained, though 'beginning' is not taken uniformly: eternity concerns being with no efficient principle, aevum being with such a principle, and time act with beginning and end of duration as measured by time.
claims: Time, aevum, and eternity differ essentially by the kind of act they measure, not merely by beginning and end.
Eternity measures act with no potency (divine being); aevum measures complete act received in a potency; time measures act mixed with potency proceeding by succession.
Time is the number of motion according to before and after, completed formally by the numbering soul.
Aevum and eternity are measures by way of unity, not number.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3529.summary: Reply to the first argument. Aevum is nothing but a participated eternity, which is why the ancient authors did not care much about distinguishing aevum from eternity and Dionysius uses one for the other. Taking 'cause' and 'author' properly, God is author of eternity not by which he is eternal but of participated eternity, aevum, as he is cause of all goodness, not of his own but of that which flows from him into creatures. Less well, 'cause' can be taken broadly for whatever is prior in concept: since the divine essence is conceptually prior to its being and being to eternity, as the mobile is prior to motion and motion to time, God can be called cause of his eternity in our mode of understanding, though he is really his eternity.
claims: God is author of participated eternity (aevum), not of his own eternity.
God is really identical with his eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3532.summary: Reply to the second argument. Where there are different ways of measuring there must be different proper measures, as bread and wine are measured differently. Since different acts are measured differently, different proper measures correspond to them, though one can be ordered to another as first and exceeding measure. As divine being is the measure of all act, eternity is the measure of all duration, exceeding and not equalled. But besides it there must be other proper measures for the different modes of measuring.
claims: Eternity is the exceeding measure of all duration, but each kind of act has its own proper measure.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3535.summary: Reply to the third argument. Divine goodness is participated in different ways, and a participated perfection receives a name in two ways: by the common concept of the perfection, in which case the name is common to the communicating source and all participants by analogy (goodness, being); or by the proper mode in which it is received in a creature, as cognition is participated from God by all knowers while 'sense' is imposed to signify cognition in a determinate mode and so is not common to all. Likewise 'eternity' names duration in the mode in which it is in its source, so other participated durations are not called eternity.
claims: 'Eternity' names duration in its source's mode, so participated durations do not share the name.
concepts: common vs. proper names of perfections

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3539.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Time is per se the measure of the first motion, so temporal things' being is measured by time only as it is subject to variation from the heavens' motion. The Commentator says we sense time as we perceive ourselves to be in variable being from the heavens' motion. So everything ordered to the heavens' motion as cause, whose first measure is time, is measured by time, and whoever senses any variability following from the heavens' motion senses time, even without seeing that motion.
claims: Temporal things are measured by time only as subject to variation from the heavens' motion.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3542.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Although the act measured by aevum is all at once without succession, its being is from another, and this distinguishes aevum from eternity (Dist. 8).
claims: Aevum differs from eternity by measuring received being.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3554.summary: First argument that the 'now' of eternity is not eternity itself. The now of eternity, of time, and of aevum seem to be one, as when we say 'when motion is, the angel is and God is'. Eternity is not time, so the now of eternity, being the same as the now of time, is not eternity.
claims: The 'now' seems common to time, aevum, and eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3557.summary: Second argument. Every now is indivisible, but eternity is divisible, as Lombard's text cites 'your years are from generation to generation', speaking of the duration of eternity.
claims: Scripture speaks of the 'years' of eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3563.summary: Third argument. The standing now makes eternity (Boethius), so the now is the cause of eternity, and nothing causes itself.
claims: Boethius: the standing now makes eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3567.summary: Fourth argument. The now of eternity relates to eternity as the now of time to time, and the now of time is not time, as a point is not a line.
claims: The now of time is not time.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3570.summary: Sed contra. Eternity is God himself, and in the divine essence there is no real diversity, so the now of eternity and eternity do not differ.
claims: Eternity is God, in whom there is no real diversity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3573.summary: Thomas's determination. According to the Philosopher, time is the measure of motion and the now of time the measure of the mobile thing. As the mobile is the same in substance throughout the motion but varies in being (Socrates in the market is other than himself at home), so the now is the same in substance throughout the succession of time and varies only in being, by the character of before and after it takes on. As motion is the act of the mobile as mobile, being is the act of the existent as being. So whatever measure measures a thing's being, the now of that duration corresponds as measure to the existing thing itself: the aeviternal thing is measured by the now of aevum, and the being whose existence eternity measures by the now of eternity. Each duration relates to its now as each act relates to what it is the act of. The act measured by time differs from what it is the act of both really, since the mobile is not the motion, and by succession, since the mobile is a permanent, not a successive, substance. So time differs from the now of time really and by succession. The act measured by aevum, aeviternal being, differs from its subject really but not by succession, since neither has succession, and aevum differs from its now in the same way. The being measured by eternity is really the same as what it is the act of and differs only conceptually, so eternity and its now differ only conceptually: eternity regards divine being and the now of eternity regards the quiddity, which is really nothing other than its being.
claims: Each duration relates to its 'now' as an act to its subject.
Time differs from its now really and by succession; aevum differs from its now really only; eternity differs from its now only conceptually.
Eternity regards divine being; the now of eternity regards the divine quiddity, which is really identical with being.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3576.summary: Reply to the first argument. The now of eternity, of time, and of aevum are not the same. 'When motion is, the angel and God are' can signify the now of eternity, of aevum, or of time. If the now of time, motion is in it as in its proper measure, and the angel and God not as measured but by a kind of concomitance, since eternity and aevum coexist with time and do not fail. If the now of eternity, God is in it as in his proper and adequate measure, and the angel and the mobile as in an exceeding measure. If the now of aevum, it corresponds to the angel as adequate measure, to God by concomitance, and to the mobile as exceeding measure.
claims: Each 'now' is the adequate measure of its own kind of being and relates to others by concomitance or excess.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3579.summary: Reply to the second argument. Eternity is indivisible, and when it is sometimes signified in the plural, this is either because it is participated in many, especially the blessed ('into perpetual eternities', Dan. 12:3), or by reason of a lower measure to which division belongs per se, time. So 'years of eternity' means eternity under which many years could be contained as under an exceeding measure.
claims: Eternity is indivisible; plural expressions refer to participated eternity or to time contained under it.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3585.summary: Reply to the third argument. As being in our understanding follows the principles of the existent as its cause, so the measure of the existent relates to the measure of its being as cause. So the now of eternity seems conceptually to be the cause of eternity, but this shows a conceptual, not a real, diversity, as between divine being and the divine existent.
claims: The now of eternity is only conceptually prior to eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-d1e3589.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The relation of time to the now of time is not like that of eternity to the now of eternity, for the reason given.
claims: The analogy of point and line does not hold for eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 introduces the bases of equality (eternity and magnitude, with power deferred) and announces two articles on eternity: what it is in reality, and how its 'now' relates to it.

ta-l1d19q2-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks what eternity is in reality. Thomas rejects the distinction of time, aevum, and eternity by beginning and end alone and grounds their difference in the kinds of act they measure. Eternity measures act with no potency, divine being and operation. Aevum measures complete act received in a potency. Time measures act mixed with potency, proceeding by succession, and is the number of motion according to before and after, completed formally by the soul. Aevum is participated eternity, God is really his eternity, and eternity is the exceeding measure of all duration while each act has its proper measure.
claims: Eternity, aevum, and time differ by the kind of act they measure.
Aevum is participated eternity; God is his eternity.

ta-l1d19q2-Dd1e3546.summary: Article 2 asks whether the 'now' of eternity is eternity. Thomas holds that each duration relates to its now as an act to its subject. Time differs from its now really and by succession, and aevum differs from its now really only. Eternity differs from its now only conceptually, since divine being is really identical with the divine quiddity. The nows of time, aevum, and eternity are distinct, each the adequate measure of its own being, and eternity is indivisible.
claims: The now of eternity is really identical with eternity, differing only conceptually.

ta-l1d19q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 19 treats eternity as a basis of the persons' equality. Article 1 holds that eternity, aevum, and time differ essentially not by beginning and end but by the kind of act they measure. Eternity measures pure act without potency, divine being. Aevum measures complete act received in a potency and is a participated eternity. Time measures successive act mixed with potency and is the number of motion completed formally by the numbering soul. God is really his own eternity. Article 2 holds that each duration relates to its 'now' as an act to its subject, so that eternity and its now differ only conceptually, while aevum and time differ really from their nows.
claims: Eternity, aevum, and time are distinguished by the kind of act they measure.
God is his eternity, and the now of eternity differs from eternity only conceptually.
Time is the number of motion completed formally by the soul.
